name: Municipality boundaries (78 municipalities)
plain: The outline of each of Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities, cut at the shoreline, with its 2020 Census population and housing units. The maps use it to draw and shade municipalities and to tell which municipality a click or a place falls in.
definition: The file municipios.geojson holds 78 shapes, one per municipality. The shapes come from the US Census Bureau's generalized county layer (a version with simplified edges, made for maps at a scale of 1:500,000), with boundaries as of January 1, 2023. The Census Bureau treats Puerto Rico's municipalities as counties. The observatory keeps the Census name, code and land area, adds the 2020 Census population and housing units, and adds its own municipality name and the tourism region.
geography: 78 municipalities, including Culebra and Vieques. 72 shapes are one polygon; 6 have several parts (Fajardo, Culebra, Mayagüez, Ceiba, Ponce, Toa Baja). Mayagüez includes Isla de Mona.

coverage.frequency: Census boundaries as of January 1, 2023. The data build re-downloads them only when run with its refresh option.

method: build.py (step_census_shoreline) pages the Census Bureau's TIGERweb layer Counties 500K for state code 72. It simplifies each shape for display (tolerance 0.0002 degrees, about 22 m) and joins population and housing units from the 2020 Census county layer by GEOID (all 78 codes match). The build uses the unsimplified shapes to place each tourism place in a municipality (a test of whether the pin lies inside the shape). A pin outside every shape is given the municipality whose shape is nearest (muni_locate.py).
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County MapServer layer 11 (Counties 500K, https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/Generalized_ACS2023/State_County/MapServer/11): shapes, NAME, GEOID, AREALAND. TIGERweb tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 82 (Counties, 2020 Census): POP100, HU100.
how_to_read: Use it to see where a municipality starts and ends on land. Do not use it to measure area or to decide whether a particular lot lies inside a municipality.
caveats: The Census Bureau generalizes these shapes (1:500,000) and the observatory simplifies them again by about 22 m, so edges can differ from larger-scale maps by more than 22 m.
Shapes stop at the shoreline. The Census Bureau's legal 2020 boundaries reach into the sea; see boundaries.shoreline_clipped.

The population and housing units are 2020 counts attached by code to shapes with boundaries as of January 1, 2023. The shapes themselves are not the 2020 polygons. Cite the shapes as 2023 and the counts as 2020.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 324 of the 24,209 counted tourism places (1.3%) have a pin outside every municipality shape, and so do 348 of the 32,541 listings in the places file. That build gave each the municipality with the nearest center point, which can be the wrong municipality near a boundary. From the next full build each takes the municipality whose shape is nearest, which moves 60 of the drawn listings (59 of them counted).

name: Barrios (901 Census county subdivisions)
plain: The 901 barrios of Puerto Rico, the sub-municipal districts the Census Bureau calls county subdivisions, with counts of tourism places inside each one. The map draws them as dashed outlines you can click.
definition: The file barrios.geojson holds 901 shapes in the 78 municipalities. Each is a county subdivision from the US Census Bureau's generalized layer (a version with simplified edges, made for maps at a scale of 1:500,000), with boundaries as of January 1, 2023, cut at the shoreline. In the Census layer 827 are barrios and 74 are barrios-pueblo, the barrio that holds a town center. The file itself does not mark which is which. The observatory adds eleven attributes: name, municipality, Census code, area, six counts of tourism places and one density.
geography: 901 barrios in 78 municipalities, from 1 barrio in Florida to 31 in Ponce. 892 shapes are one polygon; 9 have several parts (Cabezas, Machos, Arecibo, Flamenco, Playa, San Isidro, Fraile, Sabanetas, Palo Seco).

coverage.frequency: Outlines: Census boundaries as of January 1, 2023, re-downloaded only when the build is run with its refresh option. Counts: rebuilt with each snapshot.

method: build_barrios in landuse.py pages TIGERweb layer 7 (county subdivisions) for state code 72, keeps each polygon's name and code, counts the tourism places inside each polygon, simplifies the polygon for display (tolerance 0.0003 degrees, about 33 m) and rounds coordinates to 5 decimals. Area is measured on the unsimplified polygon. See boundaries.barrio_selection and boundaries.barrio_stats.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD MapServer layer 7 (County Subdivisions 500K, https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/Generalized_ACS2023/Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD/MapServer/7). The count of 827 barrios and 74 barrios-pueblo comes from the layer's LSADC field (legal/statistical area description code, read on 2026-10-03); barrios.geojson does not carry that field.
how_to_read: Click a barrio on the map for its area, tourism places, places per km², places in a flood hazard area, places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable (and of a frequent stop) and places within 400 m of any mapped stop. The lodging count is in barrios.geojson only. Compare barrios by places per km², not by raw counts: with boundaries as of January 1, 2023, areas run from 0.09 to 64 km².
caveats: A barrio is a Census statistical unit. It is not a neighborhood, a community (comunidad) or an electoral unit, and its edges do not follow the street grid.
Barrio names repeat. Use the code (geoid) to tell barrios apart; see boundaries.barrio_name.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 325 of the 24,209 counted tourism places (1.3%) have a pin outside every barrio polygon, so barrio counts add up to less than the municipality counts. Almost all are pins at or just off the coast. Measured on the original (unsimplified) shapes, 323 of the 325 lie outside the shoreline polygons of the municipalities. Measured on the published shapes, about 290 are within 100 m of a barrio polygon.
The outlines are the Census Bureau's Generalized ACS 2023 version, with boundaries as of January 1, 2023. They are not 2020 Census boundaries; cite them as 2023.
The file calls the place count assets. It counts listed tourism places, not financial or physical assets, and not other kinds of business.
Counts describe listings in Overture Maps, not visitors, sales or capacity.

name: Shoreline-clipped boundaries versus 2020 legal boundaries
plain: The observatory draws municipalities and barrios up to the shoreline, not out to sea. The Census Bureau's legal 2020 boundaries run into the ocean, so using them would put offshore points inside a municipality and count sea as part of its area.
definition: The 2020 Census county layer holds legal boundaries. They extend into coastal water, typically about 3 nautical miles (5.6 km) offshore. Across the 78 municipalities the layer's own fields report about 8,870 km² of land and 4,920 km² of water, and its polygons enclose about 13,800 km². The generalized 500k layer used for display, for municipality lookup and for barrios is cut at the shoreline; its polygons enclose about 8,900 km².

coverage.frequency: Fixed by the Census layers used

method: Shoreline-clipped polygons (Generalized_ACS2023 layers) are used for the map, for placing every tourism place in a municipality, and for the barrio layer. The 2020 county layer (legal boundaries) is read only for its attributes: POP100, HU100 and, in municipalities.json, land_km2. A place whose pin lies outside every shoreline polygon is given the municipality whose polygon is nearest (muni_locate.py, called by make_muni_locator in build.py). Until the 2026-11 fix it was given the municipality with the nearest center point in municipalities.py. In the barrio layer such a place is not counted.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 and Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD layer 7 (shoreline-clipped); tigerWMS_Census2020 layer 82 (legal boundaries). Areas in the text are sums over the 78 municipalities.
how_to_read: Municipality land areas (AREALAND, land_km2) count land only. Barrio areas (km2) are polygon areas that stop at the shoreline and can include some inland water. If you need a boundary that includes coastal waters, use the Census Bureau's full-resolution 2020 boundaries, not this file.
caveats: The shoreline polygons still hold some inland water such as rivers and lagoons, and the barrio area is a local approximation. With the 2023 boundaries, the 901 barrio areas add up to 8,916 km², 0.5% above the Census land area (8,869 km²). By municipality, the barrio areas add up to between 1.1% below the Census land area (Salinas) and 5.1% above it (Carolina: 123.5 km² of barrio area against 117.5 km² of land).

Pins just off the coast, such as on piers, can fall outside every polygon. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 324 of the 24,209 counted places (1.3%) fall outside every municipality polygon and took the municipality with the nearest center point (the next full build gives them the nearest polygon instead), and 325 fall outside every barrio polygon and are left out of the barrio counts; 323 places are in both groups.
The Census Bureau's own land area (AREALAND) is a separate figure from polygon area; see boundaries.municipio_land_area.

name: Simplified display geometry
plain: The shapes published for the maps are simplified copies. They are fine for drawing, not for measuring. The build does its place counts and barrio areas on the original shapes, and takes land-use areas from the Plan's own area attribute.
definition: Each layer is simplified before it is published, with a tolerance in degrees (1 degree of latitude is about 111 km) and rounded coordinates. Municipalities: tolerance 0.0002 degrees (about 22 m), up to 6 decimals. Barrios: 0.0003 degrees (about 33 m), 5 decimals. Land use (Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015): 0.001 degrees (about 110 m), 4 decimals. Simplification removes detail and keeps each shape valid (it does not cross itself).
method: build.py (simplify_fc) and landuse.py (build_barrios, build_landuse) call the Shapely simplify function with preserve_topology=True, which keeps each shape valid but does not keep it aligned with its neighbors. Tests of whether a place's pin lies inside a shape use the full-detail shapes. Land-use area shares use the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute, not the polygons. Barrio km² is measured on the full-detail barrio polygon. The 2D map leaves water and road polygons out of its drawing; the file keeps them.
source_detail: Code: build.py simplify_fc; landuse.py build_barrios, build_landuse
how_to_read: If you measure an area or a distance on the published polygons, expect errors of the size of the tolerance. For the land-use layer that is about 110 m, which is large for small parcels.
caveats: Small islands, narrow strips and thin barrios lose detail.
Each shape is simplified on its own, so neighboring shapes can show thin gaps or overlaps along shared edges.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, a recount on the published barrio shapes does not match the observatory's counts. Of the 24,209 places, it puts 365 in no barrio (the observatory's count is 325), 17 in two barrios and 96 in a different barrio. Use the published counts, not a recount.
Numbers in the dictionary that come from the Plan layer's own area attribute will not match an area measured on the published polygons.

name: How the barrios were chosen
plain: The observatory uses the Census Bureau's county subdivisions as barrios. They are a US Government work with no US copyright, and each has a unique 10-digit Census code. The observatory does not use data from the Centro de Recaudación de Ingresos Municipales (CRIM, the Municipal Revenue Collection Center), because the license text on its services restricts redistribution.
definition: Barrios are the county subdivisions of Puerto Rico in the Census Bureau's generalized layer (TIGERweb Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD, layer 7), selected with the filter STATE = 72. For boundaries as of January 1, 2023, the query returns 901 features of two types: barrio and barrio-pueblo. The Census Bureau also defines finer units (subbarrios) in a separate layer; the observatory does not use them.
method: fetch_barrios in landuse.py requests the layer in pages of 500 features with the fields GEOID and BASENAME and keeps the result for later builds, which download it again only when run with the refresh option.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD MapServer layer 7 (https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/Generalized_ACS2023/Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD/MapServer/7). The split into 827 barrios and 74 barrios-pueblo comes from the Census LSADC field (legal/statistical area description code), read from the layer on 2026-10-03; barrios.geojson does not carry that field. The CRIM license text was read on 2026-10-01 in the license information of its Catastro Digital service items.
how_to_read: Treat the 901 barrios as Census units. If you need the barrio list that a municipal or planning office uses, check that office's own list; it may differ.
caveats: CRIM's administrative boundaries layer lists 902 barrios (read on 2026-10-01); the Census layer has 901.
Of the 74 barrios-pueblo (town centers), 73 are named like their municipality. In six municipalities the barrio around the town has the same name as the barrio-pueblo, for example Lajas.

name: How barrio statistics are computed
plain: Barrio counts add up tourism places. They use the same place list and filters as the municipality statistics: places from Overture Maps (an open map database) with a confidence score of 0.50 or higher, without places of worship. A place counts in the barrio whose polygon contains its map pin.
definition: Place basis: listings in places.json with confidence of 0.50 or more and a type other than Places of Worship. A pin is the latitude and longitude of the listing in the source. A place counts in the barrio whose polygon contains its pin; a place whose pin lies inside no barrio polygon is not counted in any barrio. For each counted place the barrio gets six tallies. assets: one for every place. sfha: one if the place lies in a Special Flood Hazard Area of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). transit: one if the nearest mapped stop of any kind (stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal) is 400 m or less away in a straight line. lodging: one if the place is in the ACCOMMODATIONS category. acc_cur400: one if the nearest stop with a current timetable is 400 m or less away. acc_freq400: one if that is so and the busiest stop with a current timetable within 400 m has 20 or more weekday calls. km2 is the polygon area. assets_per_km2 is assets divided by km2.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build. The nightly transit refresh does not rebuild barrios.geojson.

method: build_barrios in landuse.py tests each place against the unsimplified barrio polygons with a within test and uses the first polygon found. The place's barrio name is also written to places.json:barrio. km2 = polygon area in square degrees x (111.32 x cos(latitude of the centroid)) x 110.57, which treats the polygon as flat and scales it for its latitude (see boundaries.barrio_km2). assets_per_km2 uses the unrounded area and is rounded to 2 decimals.
source_detail: Overture Maps places; FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (SFHA_TF = T); transit stops from the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and municipal timetable feeds (General Transit Feed Specification, GTFS) and from OpenStreetMap; Census TIGERweb county subdivisions
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the basis is 24,209 places island-wide. Of these, 23,884 have a pin inside a barrio polygon and are counted, and 325 (1.3%) have a pin inside none. Barrio totals are close to, but not equal to, municipality totals. In municipalities.json, 41 municipalities have more places than their barrios add up to, one has one fewer, and 36 match. San Juan differs most (3,424 places against 3,373 in its barrios).
caveats: A barrio's municipality comes from its Census code; a place's municipality in places.json comes from the municipality polygon. A place near a boundary can therefore be in one municipality and in a barrio of the next. In the 2026-10 snapshot, this is why Caguas shows one more place in its barrios (840) than in its municipality total (839): one place filed under San Lorenzo falls in a Caguas barrio.

The file calls the place count assets. It counts listed places, not financial or physical assets. Only listings the observatory classes as gastronomy, attractions, accommodations or visitor services are counted; other businesses are not.
The count of places with a mapped transit stop (transit) includes stops from expired timetables and volunteer-mapped stops. The counts acc_cur400 and acc_freq400 leave them out.
These are counts of listed places. They do not measure visitors, spending, building area or flood damage.

The barrio counts keep the values of the last full build. The nightly refresh updates places.json and municipalities.json but not barrios.geojson, so between full builds the barrio transit counts can lag them. In the 2026-10 snapshot the three transit counts equal the counts of the places of each barrio in places.json and place_access.json.

name: Municipality name (observatory spelling)
plain: The municipality's name as the observatory spells it, with accents (for example Mayagüez). Files that list places and municipalities use it to match their rows; the yearly series files use the 5-digit Census code (GEOID) instead.
definition: The Census name with the word Municipio removed, matched without regard to accents or capitals to the observatory's list of 78 municipalities (municipalities.py). The list's spelling is stored. municipalities.json, places.json and barrios.geojson use the same spelling. The yearly series files (economy_series.json, housing_series.json) use the 5-digit GEOID instead.
method: build.py (MUNI_BY_NORM) lower-cases the Census name, strips accents and looks it up in the observatory's list.
source_detail: Census Bureau name (NAME) matched to the observatory's own list of municipalities
how_to_read: Use this field to match rows between the place and municipality files. The land-use file uses the same spelling for 78 of its 79 municipality values; one water polygon carries the variant Guayanabo (see land.municipio).
caveats: Names are text with accents. Joins that strip accents on one side only will fail.

name: Municipality name (Census Bureau)
plain: The municipality's name as the Census Bureau writes it. It always ends in the word Municipio.
definition: The NAME field of the Census Bureau's county layer. All 78 values end in the word Municipio.
method: Copied from the Census layer. The build keeps the field so that readers can match the file to Census Bureau tables.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11, field NAME
how_to_read: Use it to match Census Bureau tables. For joins inside the observatory, use the observatory spelling (municipality) or the code (GEOID).
caveats: Names are a weaker match than codes: spellings, accents and the word Municipio can differ between sources. To match Census Bureau tables, use the code (see boundaries.municipio_geoid).

name: Municipality code (Census GEOID)
plain: A five-digit Census code that identifies the municipality: 72 for Puerto Rico followed by three digits for the municipality. Barrio codes start with it.
definition: GEOID is the Census Bureau's geographic identifier. For a municipality it is the 2-digit state code 72 plus the 3-digit county code. Codes run from 72001 to 72153. Each barrio's geoid begins with the GEOID of its municipality.
method: Copied from the Census layer. The build matches it to the 2020 Census layer to attach population and housing units, and uses its first five digits to find a barrio's municipality.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11, field GEOID
how_to_read: Use the code to join Census Bureau tables or other federal data. It stays the same when a name is spelled differently.
caveats: Keep it as text, as the Census Bureau does. If one table holds the code as text and the other as a number, a join will not match.
example: 72127 is San Juan; 72049 is Culebra; 72147 is Vieques

name: Municipality land area (Census, square meters)
plain: The land area of the municipality in square meters, as the Census Bureau reports it, without water. Divide by 1,000,000 for square kilometers.
definition: AREALAND from the Census Bureau's generalized county layer (a version with simplified edges, made for maps at a scale of 1:500,000), with boundaries as of January 1, 2023: the land area inside the municipality, in square meters, not counting water.
method: Copied from the Census layer without change.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11, field AREALAND
how_to_read: Use it as the denominator for density when you work with this file. 1 km² equals 1,000,000 m². With boundaries as of January 1, 2023, the 78 values add up to 8,869 km². The smallest is Cataño (12.5 km²) and the largest is Arecibo (326.2 km²).
caveats: municipalities.json holds a second land area (land_km2) taken from the 2020 Census layer. The raw values differ for all 78 municipalities, by at most 0.26 km² in 77 of them and by 1.07 km² in Manatí. After rounding to one decimal, 37 municipalities still differ. Places per km² in municipalities.json uses the 2020 value.
This is the Census Bureau's land area, not the area of the drawn polygon.
example: Cataño: 12515854 m² (12.5 km²), boundaries as of January 1, 2023

name: Population, 2020 Census (boundary file)
plain: The number of people the 2020 Census counted in the municipality on Census Day, April 1, 2020. The same count is stored in municipalities.json (see municipalities.population_2020).
definition: POP100 is the total resident population of the municipality in the 2020 Census, as published in the Census Bureau's TIGERweb county layer for 2020.

coverage.frequency: Every 10 years; the observatory holds the 2020 count

method: Read from the 2020 Census county layer (not the generalized layer) and joined to the shoreline-clipped shapes by GEOID.
source_detail: TIGERweb tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 82, field POP100
how_to_read: It describes April 2020, not today. In the 2020 Census the 78 values add up to 3,285,874, the Census count for Puerto Rico. The smallest is Culebra (1,792) and the largest is San Juan (342,259). For yearly estimates, see the resident population series.
caveats: The Census Bureau applied disclosure avoidance (a method that protects privacy) to 2020 counts. See its 2020 disclosure avoidance documentation for how this affects small areas.

The Housing page's 2020 population is not this count. It is the Census Bureau's updated April 2020 base for its estimates, which includes post-census count corrections. In the 2026-10 snapshot it differs from this count by 1 to 31 people in 68 of the 78 municipalities; the island total is the same, 3,285,874. See housing.population and methods.population_vintage_break.
People are counted where they usually live, including people in group quarters such as nursing homes.
Estimates after 2020 come from a different Census program and can differ from this count.

name: Housing units, 2020 Census (boundary file)
plain: The number of homes in the municipality in the 2020 Census, whether lived in or empty. A home can be a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room.
definition: HU100 is the number of housing units in the municipality in the 2020 Census, as published in the Census Bureau's TIGERweb county layer for 2020. A housing unit is a house, apartment, mobile home or room meant as separate living quarters. Occupied, vacant and seasonal units are all included.

coverage.frequency: Every 10 years; the observatory holds the 2020 count

method: Read from the 2020 Census county layer (not the generalized layer) and joined to the shoreline-clipped shapes by GEOID.
source_detail: TIGERweb tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 82, field HU100
how_to_read: Use it for how many dwellings exist, not how many are lived in. Occupied units equal households. In the 2020 Census the 78 values add up to 1,598,159. The smallest is Culebra (1,563) and the largest is San Juan (193,244).
caveats: It counts dwellings, not households, and not tourism lodging.
Vacant units are included. A high count in a coastal municipality can include many seasonal or second homes.

In 2020 the Census Bureau held the total number of housing units exact (its privacy method adds no noise to this total), so this is a census count, not a sample estimate. The method does add small random changes to the split between occupied and vacant homes. That split is not in this field (see housing.census_vacant_units).

name: Tourism region in the boundary file (Puerto Rico Tourism Company)
plain: The tourism region the municipality belongs to, one of the seven Porta regions of the Puerto Rico Tourism Company. A tourism region is not a Census, planning or political unit.
definition: The tourism region of each municipality, the same assignment as municipalities.region (see there for the seven regions and their members). Here it is the field region of municipios.geojson.

coverage.frequency: Fixed list; updated by hand if the Tourism Company changes its regions

method: Looked up by municipality name in municipalities.py and written to municipios.geojson and municipalities.json.
source_detail: Region assignment: Puerto Rico Tourism Company, https://tourism.pr.gov/regions/ (as coded in municipalities.py). The Census layer supplies only the list of 78 municipalities; the Census Bureau is not the source of the grouping.
how_to_read: Use it to group municipalities the way the Tourism Company does. The observatory stores no regional totals: add up the municipality rows if you need them. The observatory's counts are Overture listings, not Tourism Company statistics.
caveats: Regions are tourism groupings, not compact areas: Porta del Mar runs from Loíza to Maunabo and Yabucoa and includes Culebra and Vieques, and Porta Capital runs from San Juan and Bayamón to Cayey.

name: Barrio name
plain: The name of the barrio without the word barrio. Names repeat: the same name appears in several municipalities, and a town-center barrio-pueblo can share its name with the barrio around it. Use the code to tell them apart.
definition: BASENAME from the Census Bureau's county subdivision layer. With boundaries as of January 1, 2023, the 901 barrios have 694 different names. Six municipalities (Lajas, Hatillo, Orocovis, Canóvanas, Lares, Hormigueros) have two barrios with the same name; in Lajas they are Lajas barrio and Lajas barrio-pueblo.
method: Copied from the Census layer. The full Census name (with barrio or barrio-pueblo) is not kept in the published file.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD layer 7, field BASENAME
how_to_read: Pair the name with the municipality, or better, use the geoid.
caveats: Names alone are not unique, even inside one municipality.

With boundaries as of January 1, 2023, 79 of the 901 barrios, in 73 municipalities, have the same name as their municipality (for example Cabo Rojo, Luquillo, Dorado). In 73 of them this is the barrio-pueblo that holds the town. In six municipalities (Hatillo, Orocovis, Lares, Canóvanas, Lajas, Hormigueros) it is also the name of the ordinary barrio next to the barrio-pueblo. The barrio type comes from the Census layer; the published file does not carry it.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Barrios (click inside a barrio)

name: Municipality of the barrio
plain: The municipality the barrio belongs to, spelled the way the observatory spells it.
definition: The first five digits of the barrio's geoid identify its municipality. The build converts that code to the observatory's municipality name using the 2020 Census county layer. Every barrio has a municipality; all 78 municipalities have at least one barrio.
method: build_barrios in landuse.py looks the code up in a table from municipality code to name made in build.py (fips_to_muni).
source_detail: Census Bureau code (GEOID, first five digits) matched to the municipality list
how_to_read: Use it to group barrios by municipality. It is set by the Census code, not by where tourism places sit.
caveats: A barrio sits wholly in one municipality. Tourism places near a municipality line can be listed under the neighboring municipality in places.json.

name: Barrio code (Census GEOID)
plain: A ten-digit Census code that identifies the barrio: 72 for Puerto Rico, three digits for the municipality and five digits for the barrio. It is unique, so use it to join data.
definition: The geoid of the Census county subdivision: state code 72 (2 digits), municipality code (3 digits) and county subdivision code (5 digits). All 901 values are different and all start with the GEOID of the municipality.
method: Copied from the Census layer.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD layer 7, field GEOID
how_to_read: Use it to join to Census Bureau tables for county subdivisions. The field is spelled geoid in lower case here and GEOID in the municipality file.
caveats: Keep it as text, as the Census Bureau does. If one table holds the code as text and the other as a number, a join will not match.
Codes follow the Census boundaries as of January 1, 2023; a later release may change a code or split a barrio.
example: 7212776812 is San Juan Antiguo, in San Juan

name: Barrio area (km²)
plain: The area of the barrio polygon in square kilometers. It is measured by the observatory on the shoreline-clipped shape, not taken from the Census Bureau.
definition: Area of the unsimplified shoreline-clipped polygon, in km², rounded to 2 decimals: polygon area in square degrees x (111.32 x cos(latitude of the centroid)) x 110.57.

coverage.frequency: Computed from the polygons as of January 1, 2023

method: build_barrios in landuse.py computes it from the polygon before simplification. It is a local approximation that ignores the curve of the Earth; it is good enough to compare barrios.
source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD layer 7 (polygons)
how_to_read: Use it as the denominator for places per km². It can include a little inland water. With boundaries as of January 1, 2023, the 901 values add up to 8,916 km² and run from 0.09 km² (the barrio Toa Alta, in Toa Alta) to 64.08 km² (Lapa, in Salinas).
caveats: It is not the Census Bureau's land area. The shoreline polygons keep some inland water, so a municipality's barrio areas can add up to more or less than its Census land area (with 2023 boundaries: Carolina +5.1%, Salinas -1.1%, Mayagüez -1.0%).
The area is an approximation, not a survey measurement.

name: Tourism places in the barrio
plain: How many tourism places (restaurants, attractions, lodging and visitor services) have their map pin inside the barrio.
definition: Count of listings in places.json with confidence of 0.50 or more and a type other than Places of Worship whose pin lies inside the barrio polygon. The places are gastronomy, attractions, accommodations and visitor services together.
method: See boundaries.barrio_stats. Places come from Overture Maps and carry a confidence score from the source.
source_detail: Overture Maps Places (in the 2026-10 snapshot, listing update dates run from November 2020 to September 2026); Census TIGERweb county subdivisions
how_to_read: A high count means many listed businesses and sites in that barrio. It does not say how many visitors they receive. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 23,884 places are counted in a barrio, and the count runs from 0 (24 barrios) to 1,233 (Santurce, San Juan).
caveats: The file calls this field assets. It counts listed places, not financial or physical assets, and only places the observatory classes as gastronomy, attractions, accommodations or visitor services; other businesses are not counted.
Overture coverage is uneven; barrios with few listings may have businesses that are not in the source.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, listings were last updated between November 2020 and September 2026; some businesses may have closed.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 325 places (1.3%) fall in no barrio and are not counted here.
Barrios are different sizes. Compare with places per km².

name: Tourism places per km² (barrio)
plain: Tourism places in the barrio divided by its area in square kilometers. It shows how crowded a barrio is with listed places, whatever its size.
definition: assets divided by km2, using the unrounded area, rounded to 2 decimals.
method: build_barrios in landuse.py: round(assets / km2, 2), where km2 is the unrounded polygon area.
source_detail: Overture Maps places divided by Census-based polygon area
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 0 to 322.19 (the barrio Barceloneta, in Barceloneta: 33 places in about 0.1 km²). The highest values are in small barrios. The top five are Barceloneta, Cabo Rojo, Luquillo, Dorado and Quinto (in Ponce); all but Quinto are barrios-pueblo (town centers) in the Census layer. Compare barrios of similar size.
caveats: Very small barrios can show large values from a handful of places.
The area can include some inland water, which lowers the density slightly.

Do not compare it with places per km² in municipalities.json. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the barrio value uses the observatory's polygon area, which can include inland water, and counts only the 23,884 places inside a barrio. The municipality value uses the 2020 Census land area and counts all 24,209 places.

name: Tourism places in a flood hazard area (barrio count)
plain: How many of the barrio's tourism places sit inside an area the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps as high flood risk, the area with a 1% chance of flooding in any year.
definition: Count of tourism places in the barrio (see boundaries.barrio_assets) whose pin lies inside a polygon of the Federal Emergency Management Agency's National Flood Hazard Layer with SFHA_TF = T. That is a Special Flood Hazard Area: zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99 and the coastal V zones (VE in the data).
method: Each place is tested against the flood polygons when places are flagged (point_flags in build.py). Where polygons overlap the Special Flood Hazard Area wins. The barrio adds up the flags.
source_detail: Overture places; FEMA NFHL layer 28, DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%'; Census TIGERweb county subdivisions
how_to_read: A high number means many listed places lie in an area FEMA maps as having a 1% chance of flooding in any year (about 1 in 4 over 30 years). It is not a forecast of when flooding happens, and it says nothing about the building's elevation or insurance. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 0 to 150 and add up to 4,216.
caveats: It describes the mapped hazard at the pin, not the building.
Areas outside the mapped flood zones are not necessarily safe; flood maps may be out of date.
Places in zones where FEMA has not determined the hazard, and places outside the mapped polygons, count as not in a flood hazard area.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, barrio totals (4,216) are lower than the municipality total (4,468) because 325 places fall in no barrio. Almost all of those pins are at or just off the coast, where mapped flood zones are common: 252 of the 325 are in a flood hazard area. The barrio counts therefore leave out 5.6% of flood-zone places (252 of 4,468), against 1.3% of all places (325 of 24,209).

name: Tourism places within 400 m of any mapped stop (barrio count)
plain: How many of the barrio's tourism places have a mapped bus stop, train station or ferry terminal within 400 m (a quarter mile), measured in a straight line. It counts stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped.
definition: Count of tourism places in the barrio whose nearest mapped stop of any kind (transit stop, bus stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal) is 400 m or less away in a straight line. Stops come from the ATI timetable feed (the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado), municipal timetable feeds and OpenStreetMap bus stops, bus and rail stations and ferry terminals. Taxi stands, charging stations, airports and helipads do not count. The field transit minus acc_cur400 is the number of the barrio's places within 400 m of a mapped stop but of no stop with a current timetable.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build. The nightly transit refresh does not rebuild barrios.geojson.

method: access.py finds the nearest mapped stop of any kind for each place and sets transit_400m when the distance is 400 m or less (see places.transit_400m). build_barrios in landuse.py adds up the flags of the counted places in each barrio.
source_detail: Overture places; ATI and municipal GTFS feeds; OpenStreetMap; Census TIGERweb county subdivisions
how_to_read: A high number means many places are near a mapped stop. It does not say whether buses run often or at useful hours. For places near a stop whose timetable has not ended, see acc_cur400. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 0 to 1,218 and add up to 11,429.
caveats: Distance is a straight line, not the walking route.

Stops from expired timetables and volunteer-mapped stops still count, so real service may be thinner. In the 2026-10 snapshot 131 barrios have a value above 0 but no place near a stop with a current timetable.
A barrio with no stop in the data shows 0, which can mean no data rather than no service.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, barrio totals (11,429) are lower than the island count (11,507) because 78 places near a mapped stop fall in no barrio. The barrio counts are rebuilt only at a full build; the nightly refresh does not update them.

name: Tourism places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable (barrio count)
plain: How many of the barrio's tourism places are within 400 m, in a straight line, of a stop whose published timetable has not ended.
definition: Count of tourism places in the barrio (see boundaries.barrio_assets) whose distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable (ts_m in place_access.json) is 400 m or less. A stop with a current timetable is a scheduled stop of ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or of a municipal transit system whose operator's feed had not ended on the access date of the build. The stop can lie in another barrio or municipality. The field transit minus acc_cur400 is the number of the barrio's places within 400 m of a mapped stop but of no stop with a current timetable.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build. The nightly transit refresh does not rebuild barrios.geojson, so between full builds this count can lag the municipality fields.

method: build_barrios in landuse.py adds one for each counted place (confidence 0.50 or higher, no places of worship) whose pin lies in the barrio and whose access flag cur400 is true: ts_m of 400 or less, from access.py.
source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); stops and feed end dates from transport.json and operators.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02); Census TIGERweb county subdivisions
how_to_read: A high number means many of the barrio's places are close to a stop with a timetable in force. It does not show how often vehicles come. In the 2026-10 snapshot values run from 0 to 1,210 (Santurce, San Juan) and add up to 7,723. 153 of the 901 barrios have a value above 0. The barrio total is lower than the island count (7,790) because 67 places near a stop with a current timetable fall in no barrio. Compare barrios by the share of their places (divide by assets), not by raw counts, because they differ in size.
caveats: Straight-line distance, not a walking route.
A stop with a current timetable is not proof of service. It shows that a schedule is published, not that vehicles run on time or at all. The observatory has no real-time data.
A barrio with 0 can sit in a municipality whose operator did not renew its feed, or in one with no feed. It does not show that no vehicle runs.
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing and rental cars are in no timetable, so they are not counted.
The values keep the access date of the last full build. A feed that ends later is not reflected until the barrios are rebuilt.
These are counts of listed places. They do not measure visitors, spending or capacity.

name: Tourism places within 400 m of a frequent stop (barrio count)
plain: How many of the barrio's tourism places are within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable and 20 or more weekday departures. It is a rough sign of frequent service.
definition: Count of tourism places in the barrio (see boundaries.barrio_assets) that have a stop with a current timetable within 400 m and for which the busiest such stop within 400 m has 20 or more weekday calls (ts_m of 400 or less and ts_calls of 20 or more in place_access.json). A call is one stop time in the timetable; the app calls them departures. 20 is a threshold chosen for the observatory, not a standard.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build. The nightly transit refresh does not rebuild barrios.geojson, so between full builds this count can lag the municipality fields.

source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); stops and feed end dates from transport.json and operators.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02); Census TIGERweb county subdivisions
how_to_read: A high number means many of the barrio's places have a busy stop nearby. It is a proxy for frequency, not a headway (the time between vehicles). In the 2026-10 snapshot values run from 0 to 1,205 (Santurce, San Juan) and add up to 5,120. 67 of the 901 barrios have a value above 0. The barrio total is lower than the island count (5,163) because 43 places near a frequent stop fall in no barrio.
caveats: Straight-line distance, not a walking route.
A stop with a current timetable is not proof of service. It shows that a schedule is published, not that vehicles run on time or at all. The observatory has no real-time data.
A barrio with 0 can sit in a municipality whose operator did not renew its feed, or in one with no feed. It does not show that no vehicle runs.
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing and rental cars are in no timetable, so they are not counted.
Weekday calls describe a typical Wednesday. Holidays and other exceptions in the feeds are not applied (see transit.typical_weekday).
The values keep the access date of the last full build.

name: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 (land classification layer)
group: Land-use plan: map layer and fields
plain: The Junta de Planificación's land-use plan, shown as a map. It sorts all land in Puerto Rico into urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural and specially protected rural land, plus water and roads.
definition: The file landuse.geojson holds 996 polygon features: 881 multi-part and 115 single polygons. They come from the Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT), the land-use plan of the Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico. The version is dated 30 November 2015. The shapefile's own version fields read PUT-2014 and 30-NOV-2015; the observatory calls it the Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015. Each feature is one land class within one municipality, and a class can have several features in a municipality. Five attributes are kept: class code (cls), class name (label), group, display color and municipality (the field is named municipio).
geography: Puerto Rico: 996 polygon features across the 78 municipalities

coverage.frequency: One version, dated 30 November 2015. The build re-reads it only when run with its refresh option.

method: landuse.py (fetch_put) reads a copy of the Junta's official Plan shapefile (version of 30 November 2015) and reprojects it from the NAD83(2011) Puerto Rico State Plane projection to WGS 84. If that copy is missing, the build reads the public ArcGIS Online copy. Each polygon gets a label, group and color from the GROUPS table in landuse.py. The published file is a simplified display copy. Each place's land class is found on the full-detail polygons; area shares use the Plan layer's own Shape_Area attribute (see land.put_statistics).
source_detail: Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico, Plan de Uso de Terrenos, version of 30 November 2015. The observatory's layer is made from a copy of the Junta's official shapefile, version of 30 November 2015. A public copy of the Plan layer is hosted on ArcGIS Online (https://services6.arcgis.com/a523XM128lX5Nsff/arcgis/rest/services/Puerto_Rico_Land_Use_Plan/FeatureServer/0); it shows no owner or license text. The Junta's page for the Plan: https://www.jp.pr.gov/planificacion-fisica?tab=terrenos. Legal basis for the category names: Código Municipal (Ley 107-2020), Libro VI, Art. 6.007, and Ley 550-2004; law text at https://www.lexjuris.com/lexlex/leyes2020/lexl2020107-VI.htm (Lexjuris copy).
how_to_read: Use it for the broad pattern of where the Plan allows growth and where it protects land. The 2D map draws the four land groups and leaves water and road polygons out; they stay in the file.
caveats: The Plan dates from 30 November 2015. Land may since have been built on, reclassified or protected; the observatory does not track changes.
The Plan is a planning classification, not a zoning map. It does not say what may be built on a lot; see land.calificacion.
Polygons are simplified to about 110 m, so do not use the file to decide the class of a single lot.
On the 2D map the popup shows only the first land polygon at the click point.

This file is a simplified copy made by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) and reprojected to WGS 84. It is not the Junta de Planificación's official map; do not present it as such. The source states no data license (the Junta's site footer reserves all rights), so check the Junta's terms before reuse.

The Plan file splits some classes into several records within a municipality, by a type code (TIPO) in the Plan file that the observatory does not publish. Feature counts are not counts of zones or areas; use the area figures.

Legal basis: Art. 6.007 of the Código Municipal (Ley 107-2020) sets the three basic categories (urbano, urbanizable, rústico) for municipal territorial plans and says they must be consistent with the categories the Junta creates by regulation under Ley 550-2004, the law for the Plan de Uso de Terrenos. The state Plan uses the same category names. The summaries in this dictionary paraphrase the law and the Plan's class names; they are not legal definitions. The law cited is the law now in force; the law in force when the Plan was adopted may differ.

name: Soils (soil map units, USDA NRCS SSURGO)
plain: The soils of Puerto Rico from the soil survey of the US Department of Agriculture, shown as a map. For each area it gives the type of soil, what it formed from, how steep it is, its chemistry, and plain answers on flooding, farming and building houses.
definition: The file soils.geojson holds 802 polygon features, one or more for each soil map unit of the Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO) of the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) for Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona. A map unit is named after its main soil series, the texture of its surface layer and its slope phase (for example, Mucara clay, 40 to 60 percent slopes); the name is also given in Spanish (name_es), with the series kept and the texture and phases translated. For the main soil of each unit the file keeps the soil order of US Soil Taxonomy (order), the kind of material it formed in (origin, pm, pm_rock), the representative slope and its range (slope, slope_l, slope_h), and the chemistry of the top 30 cm (ph, om, ec, caco3). Three answers come from NRCS interpretations: farmland class (farm), limits for dwellings without basements (build) and flooding or wetness (flood).
geography: Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona: 802 polygon features

coverage.frequency: NRCS updates SSURGO once a year; the observatory reads it again only when soils.py runs with its refresh option.

method: soils.py queries Soil Data Access (keyless SQL) for the map unit polygons, components, horizons, parent material, monthly flooding, farmland class and the NRCS rating 'ENG - Dwellings W/O Basements'. The main soil is the component with the largest share of the unit; in an Urban land-<soil> complex it is the largest classified soil when it covers at least 15% of the unit, and cover names the Urban land on top with its share. Chemistry is the thickness-weighted mean of the horizons in the top 30 cm. Flooding is the most frequent monthly class of the soil described, and its drainage where it does not flood. Building limits are the rating that covers the largest share of the unit's rated components. Where the survey maps only Urban land, the USGS geologic map at 1:100,000 (Bawiec, 1998) splits it into land on young river, swamp or beach deposits (geo_wet, can flood) and land on rock or older terraces (geo_dry); Vieques and Culebra are not on that map and stay unrated. Polygons are simplified to about 10 m.
source_detail: USDA NRCS, Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO), survey areas PR682, PR684, PR686, PR688, PR689, PR700 and PR787, read from Soil Data Access (https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/). Geologic map: Bawiec, W.J., 1998, USGS Open-File Report 98-38 (https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/1998/of98-038/), map units Qa, Qs and Qb.
how_to_read: Choose what to show in the layer's menu: the soil type and what it formed from, the slope, the chemistry of the top 30 cm, or one of three questions (signs of flooding, farming, building houses). Untick a row of the legend to hide that class. Read it as the typical soil of an area for planning; the official flood zones are FEMA's, and this layer complements them.
caveats: A map unit names its typical soil; other soils, up to a large share of the unit (see share), sit inside it. Do not use it to decide what is under a single lot.
NRCS ratings are made at the scale of the survey and do not replace a study of the site by a licensed professional.
The flooding answer is the soil's own record of flooding and wetness, not a flood zone. The official flood zones are the FEMA ones (hazards.flood_zones_layer).
Under Urban land alone the answer comes from a geologic map at 1:100,000 made in 1998, not from the soil survey: it says what kind of ground the neighbourhood stands on, not how often it floods.
Water, quarries, landfills, made land and areas NRCS marks as not public information have no soil described and are shown as not rated.

name: Soil map unit: key, symbol and name (mukey, musym, name, name_es)

plain: The acidity, organic matter, salinity and lime of the top 30 cm of the soil.
definition: Thickness-weighted means over the horizons of the main soil in the top 30 cm: ph is the pH in water (1:1, ph1to1h2o_r), om the organic matter in percent of weight (om_r), ec the electrical conductivity in decisiemens per metre, a measure of salinity (ec_r), and caco3 the calcium carbonate equivalent in percent, the lime (caco3_r). geography: Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona: each soil map unit

coverage.frequency: NRCS updates SSURGO once a year; the observatory reads it again only when soils.py runs with its refresh option.

name: Signs of flooding or standing water (flood, geo)
plain: Whether the soil shows that it floods, often or at times, or stays wet; and, under Urban land alone, whether the ground below is river, swamp or beach deposits.

In a land type with no soil (salt flats, tidal swamps) the worst class of its components; in a map unit of Urban land alone, the USGS geologic map at 1:100,000: geo_wet on young river, swamp or beach deposits, with geo naming the map unit (Qa alluvium, Qs swamp deposits, Qb beach deposits), and geo_dry on rock or older terraces.

name: Land-use group: Urban land (Suelo Urbano)
plain: Land the Plan classes as urban (Suelo Urbano).
definition: Suelo Urbano (code SU). It is the urban category of the three basic categories (urbano, urbanizable, rústico) that Art. 6.007 of the Código Municipal sets for municipal territorial plans. The law does not define urban land by whether it is built. It lists what a territorial plan must do in urban land, among other things: fix gaps in existing development, support social and economic exchange, use land efficiently and keep cultural heritage. The state Plan de Uso de Terrenos, made under Ley 550-2004, uses the same category names. The group holds 1 class code (SU) and 95 features in landuse.geojson.
method: The observatory sets the group from the class code in landuse.py (GROUPS table). Group areas in municipalities.json (landuse_km2) come from the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute, summed by municipality, with water and road left out.
source_detail: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015; groups from the GROUPS table in landuse.py; legal basis for the category names: Código Municipal (Ley 107-2020), Libro VI, Art. 6.007, and Ley 550-2004; law text at https://www.lexjuris.com/lexlex/leyes2020/lexl2020107-VI.htm (Lexjuris copy)
how_to_read: In the Plan version of 30 November 2015, Suelo Urbano covers about 1,191 km², 14.2% of the 8,409 km² of mapped land. Mapped land means the four land groups, with water and roads left out; it is about 95% of the Census land area (8,869 km²). So 14.2% is not the share of the island that is built up. Areas are the sum of the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute; the published polygons are simplified and should not be used to measure them.
caveats: The Plan class does not say whether a lot is built.
The Plan dates from 30 November 2015. Land may since have been built on, reclassified or protected; the observatory does not track changes.

The group holds 11 class codes (SREP, SREP-A, SREP-E, SREP-H, SREP-EH, SREP-AH, SREP-AE, SREP-EA, SREP-AP, SREP-EP, SREP-P) and 419 features in landuse.geojson.

name: How land-use shares and place counts are computed
plain: Land-use shares for a municipality come from the Plan's own area figures, with water and roads left out. Each place listing in the places file gets the class of the Plan polygon that holds its pin; that test uses the full-detail polygons, not the published copy.
definition: Area: for each municipality the build adds the Plan layer's Shape_Area (square meters, divided by 1,000,000) by group, leaving out water and road. Shares (urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, protected_land_pct, rustic_common_pct) divide each group's area by the sum of the four land groups. landuse_km2 holds the four group areas in km². Places: every listing in places.json gets land_use (class code) and land_group from the first Plan polygon that contains its pin, or none if no polygon does. The places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct and places_urban_pct statistics in municipalities.json count listings by municipality and group.
method: build_landuse in landuse.py. Municipal areas are rounded to 0.1 km², so island-wide sums of them differ slightly from sums of the Plan's Shape_Area attribute. The percentage statistics divide by places inside any Plan polygon, including water and road polygons.
source_detail: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015; Overture Maps places
how_to_read: Use the shares for the municipality as a whole. Use the place statistics as a rough guide: they depend on where the pin is. In the Plan version of 30 November 2015, the island-wide totals of the municipal areas are 5,361 km² protected, 1,789 km² rustic, 1,190 km² urban and 68 km² urbanizable, 8,409 km² in all. Summing the Plan's Shape_Area attribute directly gives 5,361, 1,789, 1,191 and 69 km².
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the place-based statistics count all 32,541 listings, including places of worship and listings with confidence below 0.50. The other place statistics in the observatory use only the 24,209 places with confidence of 0.50 or more and no places of worship. The two bases give different results: in San Juan, 0.3% of all listings and 0.2% of the filtered places are on protected land.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 5,858 listings have their pin in a Vial (road) polygon and 172 in none, so the percentages are not shares of all places.

The Plan's Municipio field is matched by name. One water polygon is filed under the misspelling Guayanabo; it changes no figure, because water is left out of the area shares and places use their own pin location.

name: Comunidades Especiales (713 communities, 2006)
plain: The outlines of the 713 communities designated for the Comunidades Especiales program under Ley 1-2001, as the Planning Board (Junta de Planificación) drew them in 2006. Each has its name, municipality, barrio and area.
definition: The file comunidades.geojson holds one shape per community from the Junta de Planificación's 2006 delimitation of the Comunidades Especiales. 620 shapes are one polygon and 93 have several parts. The observatory keeps the name (nombre), municipality (municipio), barrio, area in km² (km2) and four inventory fields and two flood measures, each documented in its own entry.
geography: 713 communities in all 78 municipalities, from 59 in San Juan down; areas from 0.001 to 20.1 km² (median 0.16 km²)
method: comunidades.py pages the public copy of the layer, checks that every municipality name matches the observatory's list, simplifies each shape for display (tolerance 0.00005 degrees, about 5 m) and rounds coordinates to 5 decimals. Barrio names are changed from capitals to title case. km2 is the layer's Shape_Area (square metres in the Junta's State Plane projection) divided by 1,000,000, so it is measured on the original shape.
source_detail: ArcGIS Online, Comunidades_Especiales FeatureServer layer 0, fields Nombre, Municipio, Barrio, Shape_Area
how_to_read: Turn the layer on and click inside a community for its name, housing units, type and the hazards residents reported. Turn on the flood zones too to see which communities sit in a mapped flood area today.
caveats: A 2006 delimitation. Communities designated later may be missing, and some outlines may no longer match what is on the ground.
Names come from the layer as written. The barrio is the Junta's attribute and is not checked against the Census barrios the observatory draws.
A Comunidad Especial is a program designation, not a Census unit, so the observatory has no population or ACS figures for it.

name: Housing units in a Comunidad Especial (2006 inventory)
plain: How many homes the community had when the Junta de Planificación took its inventory for the 2006 delimitation.
definition: The u_vivienda field of the layer, copied without change. Empty for 10 of the 713 communities. The 703 reported values add up to 208,633 housing units and run from 6 to 4,000 (median 170).
method: Copied from the layer; a zero or empty value is published as empty.
source_detail: Field u_vivienda
how_to_read: Use it to compare the size of communities at the time of the delimitation. It is not a current count.
caveats: A 2006 figure; it does not reflect later growth, abandonment or the 2017 hurricanes.
The inventory does not say how units were counted, so it may not match Census housing units.

name: Community type (2006 inventory)
plain: How the inventory described the community, for example parcels (Parcelas), a combined community, an isolated community, an informal settlement (Arrabal) or a land invasion.
definition: The Tipo_com field of the layer, copied as written. It has 38 different spellings. The most common are Parcelas (216), Comunidad combinada (125), Comunidad aislada (77), Arrabal (49) and Invasión de terreno (45); 136 communities have no value.
method: Copied from the layer, with spaces trimmed. Spelling variants are not merged.
source_detail: Field Tipo_com
how_to_read: Read it as the inventory's description, not a legal category.
caveats: Free text: the same type appears with several spellings (for example Comunidad aislada and Comunida aislada).
Empty for 136 communities.

name: Flooding and landslides reported in a Comunidad Especial (2006 inventory)
plain: Whether the 2006 inventory recorded that the community floods (inundable) or has landslides (deslizamiento). These are what the community reported, not a hazard map.
definition: The Inundable and Deslizamie fields of the layer, turned into yes (true), no (false) or not reported (empty). Flooding: 248 yes, 452 no, 13 not reported. Landslides: 214 yes, 484 no, 15 not reported.
method: Si (in any capitals) becomes true, No becomes false, anything else stays empty.
source_detail: Fields Inundable, Deslizamie
how_to_read: Compare it with boundaries.comunidades_sfha, the share of the community inside a FEMA flood hazard area: 85 communities reported flooding but have no area in one, and 79 have area in one but did not report flooding.
caveats: Reported in 2006, before the 2017 hurricanes and later flood map updates.
Not a hazard assessment; it records what the inventory noted.

name: Area of a Comunidad Especial in a FEMA flood hazard area
plain: How much of the community's land lies inside a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, the area with a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the 100-year flood), as a percent and in km².
definition: sfha_pct is the area of the community polygon that falls inside any FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer polygon with SFHA_TF = 'T' (zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99, V and VE), divided by the community's area, times 100. sfha_km2 is km2 × sfha_pct ÷ 100. In the 2026-10 build, 248 of the 713 communities have some area in the SFHA, 95 have half or more, and 49 lie entirely inside it (99.5% or more); together 19.70 km² of community land is inside the SFHA.

coverage.frequency: Community outlines from 2006; flood zones as of the FEMA download (2026-10-06). Recomputed each time comunidades.py runs.

method: comunidades.py intersects the full-detail community polygon with the full-detail SFHA polygons (not the simplified copies the maps draw), merges the overlapping pieces so no area counts twice, and divides by the community's area. Both areas are measured in degrees², which over one community gives the same ratio as true areas. km² uses the Junta's Shape_Area, so sfha_km2 and km2 agree. A check against the simplified map copy of the flood zones, measured in kilometres, differs by more than 1 percentage point for 8 communities, at most 3.7 points (on a 0.03 km² community).
source_detail: FEMA NFHL MapServer layer 28, DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%', SFHA_TF = 'T' (2,517 polygons); the same download build.py uses (cache/fema_nfhl_pr.geojson)
how_to_read: A value of 100% means the whole community is in the mapped 1% annual chance flood area; 0% means none of it is. Combine it with housing units for a rough sense of how many homes may sit in the flood area, keeping in mind that homes are not spread evenly inside a community.
caveats: Describes the mapped hazard on the land, not the elevation, construction or insurance of any home.
The 0.2% annual chance (500-year) zone and areas FEMA has not mapped are not counted.
The outlines are from 2006 and the flood maps are more recent, so a community that grew beyond its 2006 outline is measured only inside it.

name: WCRP communities (76 community plans, approximate points)
plain: The communities that are writing or have written a resilience plan in FPR's Whole Community Resilience Planning (WCRP) program. Each one is a single dot near the community, with its name, municipality and WCRP region.
definition: The file wcrp.geojson holds one point per community in the WCRP program list of 2026-10-06: 76 communities in 30 municipalities. Several plans can share one point (73 different points), for example Villa Calma 1 and 2. The observatory keeps the community name (comunidad), municipality (municipio) and WCRP region (region: norte, este, sur, central, oeste or islas; empty for the 4 communities that no source assigns to a region), and three fields documented in their own entries.
geography: 76 communities in 30 municipalities: 28 in the norte region, 17 este, 12 sur, 10 central, 4 oeste, 1 islas and 4 without a region

coverage.frequency: List copied on 2026-10-06; updated by hand

method: wcrp.py reads wcrp_comunidades.csv: 72 rows from the WCRP-RAG list and 7 phase-1 communities from FPR's Smartsheet tracker, which the WCRP-RAG does not list yet. For each row without a point it looks, in the same municipality, for a Comunidad Especial with a similar name, then an OpenStreetMap place with the same name, then a Census barrio with the same name; Centro Urbano and Casco Urbano plans go to the town centre. FPR placed the other 29 by hand, from what each plan says about its location or, for communities without a plan yet, from the program's tracker; the CSV cites the source. The script checks that every point lies within about 100 m of its municipality.
source_detail: wcrp_comunidades.csv (columns comunidad, municipio, region); comunidades.geojson and gazetteer.json for the points
how_to_read: Use it to see where the program works and to compare with other layers, such as flood zones or the Comunidades Especiales. Do not read the dot as the community's boundary or its centre.
caveats: Each dot is approximate. The plans draw the community's area only in a PDF map, so the observatory has no outlines yet.

Three plans of the program serve a population group, not an area (people without a home in Ponce, and immigrant and vulnerable populations in Río Piedras). They are not on the map: on 2026-11-23 FPR decided that groups of people are not shown as points on a public map.
One community, Ceiba Carmelita, also reaches into Vega Baja; its dot is in Vega Alta.
El Cerro (Naranjito) has a provisional point at the town centre: no source gives its location yet.

name: WCRP plan status
plain: Whether the community's resilience plan is approved by the Puerto Rico Department of Housing or still in progress.
definition: The estado field: plan_aprobado for 59 communities and en_proceso for 17 (10 in the WCRP program list and 7 phase-1 communities from the program's tracker), as of 2026-10-06.

coverage.frequency: List copied on 2026-10-06; updated by hand

method: Copied from wcrp_comunidades.csv without change.
source_detail: wcrp_comunidades.csv, column estado

values.plan_aprobado: The Puerto Rico Department of Housing approved the community's resilience plan.
values.en_proceso: The community is still writing its plan.

how_to_read: On the map, each community is marked with the centre figure of the WCRP program logo: solid orange for an approved plan and an orange outline for a plan in progress. When several plans share a point, the marker is solid if any of them is approved; the popup lists each one with its own marker.
caveats: A snapshot of 2026-10-06. Plans approved later show as in progress until FPR updates the CSV.

name: Where a WCRP point comes from
plain: What the dot for a WCRP community is placed on, and the name of that place, so you can judge how close it is to the community.
definition: The ubicacion field gives the kind of place and referencia gives its name. In the 2026-10-06 list: 40 osm, 23 comunidad_especial, 7 pueblo, 4 barrio_censo and 2 manual.

coverage.frequency: List copied on 2026-10-06; updated by hand

method: wcrp.py fills both fields when it matches a name. When FPR places a row by hand, ubicacion still names the kind of place the point comes from, and the CSV's nota column (not published) says why and cites the plan.
source_detail: wcrp_comunidades.csv, columns ubicacion and referencia

values.comunidad_especial: A point inside the Comunidad Especial with that name (Junta de Planificación, 2006).
values.osm: The OpenStreetMap place or landmark with that name: a barrio or sector label, a school, a park or a community centre.
values.barrio_censo: A point inside the Census barrio with that name.
values.pueblo: The town centre of the municipality.
values.manual: Coordinates that the plan itself gives.

how_to_read: A comunidad_especial point is usually inside the community. An osm or barrio_censo point can be a kilometre or more away when the community is one sector of a large barrio.
caveats: None of these places is the community's own boundary. Some landmarks, such as a school the plan names, may sit just outside it.

name: Tourism places within a 400 m walk of a stop with a current timetable (barrio count)
plain: How many of the barrio's tourism places are within a 400 m walk, along mapped roads, of a stop whose published timetable has not ended.
definition: Count of tourism places in the barrio (see boundaries.barrio_assets) whose walking distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable (tw_m in place_access.json) is 400 m or less. It is acc_cur400 with the distance walked along mapped roads instead of a straight line. The stop can lie in another barrio or municipality.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build. The nightly transit refresh does not rebuild barrios.geojson, so between full builds this count can lag the municipality fields.

method: build_barrios in landuse.py adds one for each counted place (confidence 0.50 or higher, no places of worship) whose pin lies in the barrio and whose access flag walk400 is true: tw_m of 400 or less, from access.py.
source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); stops and feed end dates from transport.json and operators.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02); roads from OpenStreetMap (site/data/roads.bin, ODbL); Census TIGERweb county subdivisions
how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot values run from 0 to 1,179 (Santurce, San Juan) and add up to 6,724, against 7,723 in a straight line (acc_cur400). 143 of the 901 barrios have a value above 0. The barrio total is lower than the island count (6,787) because 63 such places fall in no barrio. Compare barrios by the share of their places (divide by assets), not by raw counts.
caveats: Along mapped roads, not every way a person can walk. The road file has no footways, paths, steps, pedestrian streets, sidewalks or crossings, and it does not know fences, gates or a road that is unsafe to cross. The visitor-access study (docs/analysis/visitor-access-2026-10) repeated the run on a full OpenStreetMap walking network: the island share within 400 m moved from 26.6% to 27.0%, and municipal shares moved a median 0.0 points (90th percentile 0.99, largest 11.3 in Hormigueros).

1,210 places (1,074 on the default basis, 4.4%) have no walkable road within 150 m and keep their straight-line distance (see place_access.tw_straight). For them the value is a lower bound: the real walk is at least that long.
A stop with a current timetable is not proof of service. A timetable is a schedule: it does not show that vehicles run on time or at all. The observatory has no real-time data.
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing, rental cars and tour shuttles are in no timetable, so they are not counted.
The values keep the access date of the last full build. A feed that ends later is not reflected until the barrios are rebuilt.
These are counts of listed places. They do not measure visitors, spending or capacity.
